newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Social Chapter, a rude dawn for British business.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Social Chapter, a rude dawn for British business.

text.p: Britain's Labour government will shortly adopt the EU Social Chapter on workers' rights, with big business warning it may open the way to costly, inflexible labour laws but trades unions hailing a new era in industrial relations.

Prime Minister Tony Blair, endorsed by a landslide win at the election on May 1, is due to sign the Social Chapter at a European Union summit in Amsterdam on June 16 after years of Conservative feet-dragging.
What the new workers' regulations mean for business in terms of cost and long-term impact remains hazy.
"The Social Chapter is all generalities, the problem is pinning it down," says Graham Bishop, European analyst at Salomon Bros International.
"Business needs: 'Here is a directive, here is a clause, this is what you have to do to your labour force which you didn't before or what you no longer have to do'", he said.
Talk to business groups and the level at which a minimum wage will be set -- another key Labour government pledge -- seems to be a much bigger concern in the medium term.

The Social Chapter, an EU framework for employment laws, so far boasts only two directives. It gives three months unpaid leave to parents after the birth of a child; and says that employees of multi-national firms must be informed of corporate changes through 'works councils'.
Many British firms working in Europe have already adopted such measures.

The Trades Union Congress (TUC), the umbrella group for British unions, says 50 British companies run works councils and another 50 are set to do so. Once the Social Chapter is signed, the TUC anticipates an additional 130 firms will be affected by the directive. The costs of implementation appear to have been minimal.
UNIONS CHAMPION SOCIAL CHAPTER
TUC general secretary John Monks is lobbying for employment to top the agenda in Amsterdam. An employment charter is likely to be included in the EU treaty.
Against a background of 18 million unemployed in Europe and poor working conditions for many, the unions are championing the Social Chapter not least for its symbolic significance.

"Ending the UK opt-out from the Social Chapter...is the first step towards a new recognition by all EU member states that social protection is as much a core policy of the (European) Union as the single market," Monks said in a speech in London.

The TUC, in effect, has called on the European workers' charter to redress the political balance in Britain's labour market. Under Margaret Thatcher's Conservative government in the 1980s, hard-hitting labour reforms curbed the right of British workers to strike, while union membership declined by a third.

"There is a great need for the Social Chapter in Britain because the UK's record on employment sticks out like a sore thumb in this part of civilised European society," TUC European spokesman Tom Jenkins said in an interview.

Jenkins is sure, however, that neither employees nor employers will get everything they want from the charter: "It's about partnership, dialogue and negotiation -- that's what the Social Chapter exists for."
European Commission president Jacques Santer reassured Britain recently that signing up to the charter would mean no new 'avalanche' of labour rules imposed on EU employers.
COMPANIES EYE COST OF NEW WORKERS' LAWS

So what's worrying many British firms? Mainly the fear that the new laws may lead to higher labour charges and a loss of flexibility for companies competing in world markets where cheap labour is still widely available.

"Entry into the Social Chapter must not result in the opening of the flood gates of social legislation from do-gooding bureaucrats in Brussels," said David Richardson, president of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC).

While opposition to Britain adopting the European legislation has turned to resignation, Reuters' survey of small to medium-sized companies, published today, shows the 16 respondents expect the charter to have a neutral to negative impact on prospects.

These findings broadly echo a Reuters poll on the eve of the May election of FTSE-100 finance directors which showed half the 20 respondents expected a neutral impact from the Social Chapter, while the others saw either a fairly negative or very negative effect.
"It's a nuisance, it's an irritation...and could damage our competitiveness on the world stage," Dr Ian Peters, the BCC's deputy director-general told Reuters.

"The worry as always is what may happen once the opt-out is removed and the rest of Europe doesn't anymore have to worry about an uneven playing field...the UK has been at a competitive advantage until now," he said.

The BCC -- which represents smaller firms which may find it harder to meet the costs of the Social Chapter -- was previously a hard-line advocate of Britain maintaining its opt-out clause. But even it appears to accept the argument has been lost.

"Business is now resigned to the fact that Britain is going to go in (to the Social Chapter). It was in the government's manifesto so there's no point in digging in our heels...We must make the best of it," Peters said.
SOCIAL CHAPTER MAY HARBOUR DANGERS

Speculation, initiated by the Conservatives in the run up to the election, that the Social Chapter could cost 500,000 jobs and run into millions of pounds (dollars) of extra bills has given way to unspecific fears among the business community about what the future holds.
Critics say the devil is in the detail still to come, including the threat that measures could be smuggled in via majority voting.
EU member states still retain a veto on matters such as social security, defence and external border controls.

But new laws on working conditions, consultation of workers or equality issues could be voted in over the heads of opponents. The EU's 48-hour average maximum work week was passed despite former prime minister John Major's Social Chapter opt-out.
"The Social Chapter potentially harbours dangers later on down the line...it all depends on what is brought forward," said the BCC's Peters, echoing the niggles of much of industry.

But the unions shouldn't get carried away with optimism either. Bishop warns the government not to make too much of the new working rights or of the EU's bid to get Europe's 18 million jobless back to work.

"The moment you say to the electorate we will solve the employment problem at the European level and then if it's not solved at that level, Europe looks daft. To make claims which can't be fulfilled is to reduce the credibility of the whole European venture," Bishop said.
